findings.title: Building the SQLite ID list performs quadratic copying
findings.body: Each iteration formats the entire accumulated ID string again, so constructing a list of N IDs copies O(N²) bytes and creates O(N²) allocation pressure. With the 32,767-ID batch size used by the new test, this can copy several gigabytes of strings for one delete batch, causing substantial CPU and GC overhead. Build the list with a `strings.Builder` or an append buffer instead.

findings.title: All cleanup jobs now run ten times more often
findings.body: Changing the ticker from ten minutes to one minute increases the frequency of every cleanup job, not just annotation cleanup. This also increases database and filesystem work for snapshots, dashboard versions, images, query history, and other jobs; if a cleanup run takes over a minute, the buffered ticker can cause runs to start back-to-back. The PR description does not explain this broader workload change.

findings.title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at error level
findings.body: This and the corresponding cleanup logs use `r.log.Error` for normal batch progress, including cases where `err` is nil (the same occurs at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579). Every successful cleanup therefore generates error-level log records, and the records include the batch's IDs. This creates misleading error noise and can trigger log-based alerts during routine cleanup.
